pool.prompt: A project site is in the NESC 'Light' loading district (zero radial ice by definition). What is the ice load (w_ice) contribution for this cable?
choices: 0 lb/ft — Light district has no radial ice loading by definition
A value proportional to cable diameter, calculated the same way as Heavy district
0.5 lb/ft, a flat default regardless of district
Ice load cannot be determined without knowing the exact cable OD
pool.explanation: The Light loading district is defined with zero radial ice thickness (t=0 in). Since the ice-load formula is proportional to ice thickness, zero thickness means zero ice load — only wind load and cable self-weight apply in this district.

pool.prompt: An ADSS cable in the Heavy loading district has OD = 0.71 in and radial ice thickness t = 0.50 in. Using the NESC ice-load formula w_ice = K x t x (D+t) with K~1.244 (lb/ft, inches), what is the approximate ice load?
choices: 0.750 lb/ft
0.377 lb/ft
0.068 lb/ft
pool.explanation: w_ice = 1.244 x t x (D+t) = 1.244 x 0.50 x (0.71+0.50) = 1.244 x 0.50 x 1.21 ~= 0.752 lb/ft. Note: the exact K constant derives from an assumed ice density (commonly cited as 56-57 lb/ft^3 depending on NESC edition), so always confirm the constant against the specific adopted NESC edition before a final design calculation.
pool.citation: NESC ice-loading formula (K constant UNVERIFIED-EXACT across NESC editions this session — verify against adopted edition).

pool.prompt: NESC Rule 250C (Extreme Wind loading) must be considered whenever any part of a pole or its conductors is how many feet or more above the ground?
choices: 40 feet
50 feet
60 feet
80 feet
pool.explanation: NESC Rule 250C requires Extreme Wind loading consideration whenever any part of a pole or the conductors attached to it is 60 feet or more above the ground. This case uses regional wind speed maps (rather than the standard three-district table) to determine the applicable wind load.

pool.prompt: In the parabolic sag formula Sag = (w x L^2) / (8 x T), what happens to sag if the span length L is doubled while all other values stay the same?
choices: Sag doubles
Sag increases by 50%
Sag quadruples (increases by 4x)
Sag is unchanged — sag is independent of span
pool.explanation: Sag is proportional to L^2. Doubling L increases L^2 by 4x, so sag quadruples — this quadratic relationship is why long spans are challenging: doubling span length from 150 ft to 300 ft quadruples the sag under the same loading and tension, often requiring much higher cable tension to stay within NESC clearance.

pool.prompt: Why does NESC's Extreme Wind rule use regional wind speed MAPS rather than the flat three-district loading table used for combined ice/wind loading?
choices: The two systems are actually identical; maps and tables produce the same result everywhere

Wind speed varies significantly by specific geography (coastal exposure, terrain, elevation) in ways the coarse three-district (Light/Medium/Heavy) table doesn't capture — a dedicated regional map (based on ASCE 7 data) gives more location-specific accuracy for the extreme-wind case, which applies to taller/more exposed structures
Regional maps are only used when ice loading is exactly zero
The three-district table was discontinued and replaced entirely by wind maps in the 2023 edition
pool.explanation: The standard three-district table (Light/Medium/Heavy) is a simplified, coarse geographic grouping for combined ice/wind design. The Extreme Wind rule (Rule 250C), which specifically targets taller/more wind-exposed structures, uses regional wind speed maps for more geographically precise wind data, since wind exposure varies more granularly than the district table captures.

pool.prompt: A 150 ft span and a 300 ft span carry identical cable at identical tension. Roughly how does the 300 ft span's sag compare to the 150 ft span's sag?
choices: Identical sag on both spans
Twice the sag on the 300 ft span
Four times the sag on the 300 ft span
Half the sag on the 300 ft span
pool.explanation: Since sag scales with span length squared (L^2), doubling the span (150 to 300 ft) quadruples the sag at the same tension and loading — a direct consequence of the parabolic sag formula.

pool.prompt: Why must a designer verify ice-loading and wind-loading district assignments specifically for the project's geographic location rather than assuming a default?
choices: District assignment has no real effect on the final design

Loading district (Light/Medium/Heavy) directly determines the ice thickness and wind pressure values used in structural calculations — using the wrong district produces an incorrectly sized/tensioned cable design that could violate NESC clearance or fail under actual local conditions
All of the continental US is assigned to the same loading district
District assignment only matters for copper cable, not fiber
pool.explanation: Loading district assignment directly drives the ice thickness (t) and wind pressure inputs to the sag/tension/clearance calculations. An incorrect district assignment produces a design that may be under-built for actual local ice/wind conditions (safety and clearance risk) or needlessly over-built (unnecessary cost).

pool.prompt: What two load types combine (along with the cable's own weight) to determine the total transverse load on an aerial ADSS cable under NESC design conditions?
choices: Wind load and ice load
Only wind load — ice load is never a factor for fiber cable
Only ice load — wind load only applies to power conductors
Chromatic dispersion and PMD, translated into a mechanical load equivalent
pool.explanation: Wind load and ice load (where the loading district specifies nonzero ice) combine with the cable's self-weight to determine the total transverse load used in sag/tension/clearance calculations — both are real mechanical loads that apply to fiber cable exactly as they do to other aerial conductors.
